en: Record of the Ordination of Bhikṣus at Mount Dinghu, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Zaiqiu.

I reverently contemplate that when the Tathāgata governed the world, he observed the capacities of sentient beings, which consist of the superior, middling, and inferior; therefore, he established the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This refers to bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas. Although the vehicles are divided into three, there is none that does not take precepts as the foundation of concentration and wisdom.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he immediately transmitted and recited the Threefold Pure Precepts of Vairocana Buddha for the sake of the great-minded bodhisattvas.
Subsequently, at the Deer Park and in the Royal City, he gradually established them for the sake of those of the two vehicles.

Regarding the five categories of offenses and the seven groups of rules, a quorum of ten monks was established to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) for conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon bhikṣus.
However, when the Buddha first appeared in the world, the True Dharma was rarely heard in the borderlands, and those who had left the household life among the fivefold assembly were also few.
At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana resided in the kingdom of Aparāntaka in Western India. There was a son of a householder named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa who left the household life and sought [ordination].
The Venerable One was to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*), but as there were not ten monks in that country, it could not be conferred. He hurried to report this to the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted that in border regions, a community of five monks who maintain the Vinaya may perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to confer full ordination;
among these five, one must be a Vinaya-holder who is well-versed in performing the rituals. Thus, the ritual master himself constitutes the fifth member. This is the instruction.
The preceptor must be well-versed in the ritual procedures. As for the other monks who serve as witnesses to the ordination, they must be pure;

only then may they be permitted to act as witnesses. Regarding what is meant by "central" and "borderland": the central region refers to Central India (Madhyadeśa), which lies at the center of the four regions of India—east, south, west, and north.
As for the borderlands (*pratyantajanapada*): traveling east from Central India to its limit, there is the country of Bābīkṛta; beyond that country is [the borderland].
To the south, reaching the southern limit, is the Stūpa of Tranquil Virtue; outside this stūpa lies the borderland.
To the west, reaching the western limit, is Mount Ṛṣigiri of the Sage Śaila; outside this mountain lies the borderland.
To the north, reaching the northern limit, is the Kingdom of Yūpārāja; outside this kingdom lies the borderland. This present-day China lies to the east of Pārvatīya, five *yojanas* from India.
It is over seven thousand *li* away. For more than one thousand years since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, the Buddha-dharma had not been heard there.

Until the third year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Emperor was moved by an auspicious dream; he then dispatched eighteen men, including General Cai Yin, as envoys to the Western Regions to seek the Way of the Buddha.
In the sixth year, Yin and his party reached the kingdom of Yuezhi and encountered the two [monks], Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
The Dharma Master obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra consisting of six hundred thousand words. Together they returned to the East. Emperor Ming was greatly pleased;
consequently, the kings, ministers, officials, and commoners of this land gradually came to know of and turn toward the faith.

In the fourteenth year, Liu Jun, the Minister of Works and Marquis of Yangcheng, along with over one thousand officials, scholars, and commoners, entered the monastic order. This included Lady Yin and Lady Wang Jieyu.
...and so forth. He granted ordination to two hundred and thirty women from the palace. At that time, the two Dharma Masters ordained these people;
they shaved their hair and beards, donned the *kaṣāya* robes, and were given only the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Precepts.
Because it was not possible to bestow the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon fewer than ten or five persons, [the tradition continued] until the tenth year of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty. (100)
Within the following years, the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Precepts were still being transmitted one to another.
In the first year of the Jianning era of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, five śramaṇas from North India arrived in the land of Han to confer the full ordination (mahā-śīla) upon monks.
Their names were: first, Zhi Falin; second, Zhi Qian; third, Zhu Fahu; fourth, Zhu Daosheng; and fifth, [the fifth name].

At that time, the Mahāvinaya did not yet exist [in Chinese]. Zhi Falin orally recited and produced one fascicle of the *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Text) and one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Formulas), which circulated here.

In the second year of the Jiaping era (249 CE) of the early Wei dynasty (during the reign of Emperor Shao Ling Gong), the Śramaṇa Dharmakāla (translated as "Dharma-Time") from Central India—who was well-versed in reciting the various Vinayas—arrived at Luoyang and established the *Karmavācanā*.

Regarding the ritual for receiving the precepts (*śīla*), ten monks were required according to the established rule. Thus, the Buddha-dharma spread extensively throughout China, marking the beginning of the reception of the Vinaya in the Eastern Land (China).
Later, in the second year of the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin dynasty, the Indian *śramaṇa* Dharmadatta (translated here as Fǎhǎi) arrived.
He translated three versions of the *Śāriputra-vinaya-mātṛkā*. In the fourteenth year of the Jianyuan era, Zhu Fannian translated the ten-fascicle *Vinaya* (Pi nai ye lü).
In the tenth year of the Hongshi era of Yao Xing of the Later Qin, the Indian Venerable Vimalākṣa [arrived].

(Also known as Wugouyan), came to travel in the region east of the Passes and propagated the Vinaya. It was due to the efforts of Kumārajīva that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*—a great practice—was translated;

however, it was the work of [Faxian] that it was widely practiced. In the eleventh year of Hongshi, the Venerable Buddhayaśas from Central India arrived and translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*.
While the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was previously practiced in Guanzhong, it became prevalent in Jiangnan.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* reached the Yuan-Wei dynasty. It was the Vinaya Master Fachong who first propagated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* school.
Cong transmitted it to Daofu; Fu transmitted it to Huiguang; Guang transmitted it to Yunhui and Huiyuan; Yuan transmitted it to Yinyue and Hongyun;
Yun transmitted it to Hongzun; Zun transmitted it to Zhishou; Shou transmitted it to Daoxuan; Xuan transmitted it to Fali and Manyi; Yi transmitted it to Facheng; and Cheng transmitted it to Daliang.
Daosheng. Liang transmitted it to Daoyun (one). Dao’an. Huicheng. Cheng transmitted it to Huichin; all of them received it through oral transmission, reaching the innermost depths of the teaching.

From this point onward, it spread widely (as recorded in detail in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*). Until the Song and Yuan dynasties, there was never a lack of practitioners from generation to generation.

Toward the end of the Yuan and the beginning of the Ming, the observance of the precepts became somewhat different. By the middle of the Ming, those well-versed in the Vinaya were already rare. By the time of the late Ming—
One school of the Vinaya has been swept away. Since receiving full ordination, I have read the Great Vinaya Piṭaka for several years without closing my eyes, yet I could not grasp its central tenets.
Consequently, I traveled everywhere to seek out those of clear wisdom, but there was not a single person who studied the Vinaya.
As the Sūtra says: "The Vinaya Piṭaka is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma. The Vinaya Piṭaka...
The Buddha-dharma abides, yet I feared that other teachings might not endure for long. Day and night I was filled with sorrow, unable to find peace within myself.

At the age of thirty-four, I conceived the intention to travel to India to invite several Indian monks back to China, so that the precepts might be transmitted once more, causing the lamp of the precepts that had been extinguished to blaze anew, and the thread of life that had become faint to be continued again.
Thus, in the spring of the Jiashen year, he arrived at the land of Min.

Intending to hire men and provisions for a sea vessel, he planned to sail from the coast of Min for over one year to reach the eastern corner of India, the kingdom of Tamralipti, some sixty-odd stations away, and eventually arrive at Nālandā Monastery in Central India.
Unexpectedly, as the times were turbulent and the world had undergone great upheaval, his wishes were not fulfilled; thus, this year has passed in antiquity.

Rare indeed! I still lament that there was no such opportunity in the past. Recently, I have observed that when various monastic communities bestow the precepts upon others, they do not follow the Buddha’s regulations;

these are entirely unlawful and constitute a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*). What makes them unlawful? They are ignorant of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and three proclamations).

They merely transcribe the spurious compositions of others, chanting idle prose, or even create their own texts based on the teacher's personal whims. Regarding those who receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), this is the Buddha’s regulation: [the rest of the passage follows].
At most, only three people are permitted to share a single altar; if there are more, it immediately becomes an illegal act (*adharma*).

Even if one follows the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), if the recitation of the text is stilted and the proceedings contain many errors, it is still illegal—how much more so for those who compose their own fabrications? What constitutes a "separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*)?
They did not know how to establish a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) or a boundary for the precept-platform (*sīmaṇḍala*) according to the Vinaya.

Since there was no precept-platform, even when a single person received full ordination, all the co-resident bhikṣus—whether numbering a hundred or a thousand—were required to assemble together to confer the ordination upon him.

If even one bhikṣu failed to assemble, it was termed a "separate assembly" (*pṛthag-jana*). When the assembly incurs an offense, the recipient likewise does not obtain the precepts, yet he continues to receive a provisional status for the rest of his life.
One who is called a bhikṣu yet receives offerings from the faithful in vain, and openly acts as a senior elder receiving the prostrations of others—no sin is greater than this.

Or, if one performs *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) before laypeople or *śrāmaṇeras*, bestowing the [precepts] all at once upon thirty or twenty people simultaneously, this greatly violates the Buddha’s regulations.
If one does not rely on the Buddha’s teachings, how can one be said to be "born from the Buddha’s mouth" or "born through transformation by the Dharma"? O world!
There are no two Buddhas, nor are there two systems of Dharma regulation. To treat what is not the Dharma as the Dharma is to transmit error through error;

thus, following one another in succession, they fail to perceive their own faults. This is truly the extinction of the Dharma during the Age of Dharma-Decline (*mappō*). Nevertheless, this matter concerns the gateway to the Dharma no small amount.
If there are those who have received the precepts in accordance with the Dharma, they should naturally cherish them as they would protect a bright pearl. As for those who dwell therein...
Those who uphold and propagate the lineage should especially adhere to the teachings of the *vinaya*.

Relying on the Dharma, relying on the Vinaya, and relying on what the Buddha has prescribed, they shall cause the pearl of the precepts to shine brightly through the long night and ensure that the *vinaya* remains firm for all time. Such individuals are the great beings (*mahāsattva*) who propagate the True Dharma and transmit the teachings.
(The *maṇḍala* is the site of ordination; it is demarcated within the Great Boundary. Its various rites and procedures are as explained in the relevant commentaries.)

The above is a brief preface concerning the origins of receiving the precepts. Below, I shall record the names of the Preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the Ācārya, and the venerable witnesses of the Saṃgha who presided at the ordination platform;

furthermore, I shall note my own birth year, as well as the specific date, month, year, and time of receiving the precepts, so that the seniority of the *kaṭhina* (precept age) may be recognized and the ritual procedures of the ceremony may be understood.
Bhikṣu [Name], born on the [day] of the [month] in the [year], at the [time], of the [clan/family name];
a native of the [prefecture] and [county]. On the [day] of the [month] in the [year], he received the precepts and left the household life under Master [Name].
On the [day] of the [month] in the [year], at the [time], he relied upon...
The Upādhyāya received the śrāmaṇera precepts on the [day] of the [month] of the [year] at [time];
the Upādhyāya received the full ordination on the [day] of the [month] of the [year] at [time]; [he] received the Bodhisattva precepts on the [day] of the [month] of the [year] at [time];
the Karmācārya who presided over the *karmavācanā* was [name], whose Dharma-name is [name].
The Preceptor Ācārya’s Dharma Name: [Name] Dharma Title:
Venerable Saṃgha Virtuous One (Bhadanta) Virtuous One Virtuous One Virtuous One Virtuous One Virtuous One Virtuous One Virtuous One
A Brief Ritual for the Procedure:
One who has newly received full ordination (*upasampadā*) is not yet able to peruse the entire *Vinaya-piṭaka*.

Their preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and instructor (*ācārya*) should provide them with the *Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra*, causing them to read it thoroughly so that they may know how to maintain and uphold it, ensuring they do not commit any transgressions, and so that they recognize the [rules of] distribution.

The *poṣadha*, the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the reception of days, the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the receiving of robes, the relinquishing of robes, the pure gift (*viśuddhi-dāna*), and other such dharmas.
○ Regarding the *poṣadha* dharma:
every half-month, during the *poṣadha*, one should recite the precepts. Even if there are as few as four bhikṣus present, one person should be instructed to chant them.
Regarding the *Prātimokṣa*: if there are fewer than four persons, and only two or three are present, they shall perform the *poṣadha* face-to-face (*pratyakṣam*).

With the exception of the four root offenses (*mūlāpatti*), for any other transgressions of the various categories, one must, according to the Vinaya, confess before a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu; only after this may the *poṣadha* be performed.
The Method for the Face-to-Face Poṣadha:
On the day of the Poṣadha, if there are three persons, they shall each face one another and perform the ritual: baring their heads, removing their sandals, and joining their palms.
They kneel facing one another. First, the senior monk speaks as follows:
"Venerable sirs, attend with one mind. Today is the tenth day of the month for the Saṃgha to recite the precepts. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure."

(Recite three times. The latter two [recitations] are also spoken in this manner. If there are only two persons present, omit the first two characters [“Venerable Sir”] and simply say “Virtuous One. The remaining phrasing is the same as above).
○ The Method for the Mindful Recitation of the Poṣadha (If one is alone, one should speak both mentally and verbally):
"Today, on the [tenth/fourteenth/fifteenth] day, the Saṃgha of monks recites the precepts. I, bhikṣu [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times.)

If one is not pure, one should first perform a formal confession before a pure person; only then should one proceed according to the rules for purity. If one is not pure yet claims to be pure, one further commits the offense of lying.
The Method for the *Pratyekasīmā* (Face-to-Face) Retreat (the earlier retreat;
on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, one should address a Dharma-knowing bhikṣu, speaking as follows).

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am observing the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) at this monastery (if it is within a village and not a monastic residence, one should say 'in such-and-such village';
if it is in a separate room of a temple, one should say 'in such-and-such room'). Because the dwelling is dilapidated, I shall repair it.
(Recite this three times. The other should say: "Excellent. (The petitioner should reply: "Very well. (If one is observing the retreat elsewhere than in a monastery, omit the last two sentences.)

If one has personal matters concerning the Three Jewels, or matters involving one's two teachers or parents, such that one cannot join the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (fore-summer) retreat, one may enter the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* on the sixteenth day of the fifth month; this should be called the "latter three months.

Alternatively, one may enter the intermediate *anvārambhaṇa*, which lasts from the seventeenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, observing it daily according to its commencement; this is termed the "intermediate *anvārambhaṇa*."
○ The Method for Mindful Meditation on the Summer Retreat (If there is no person upon whom one relies, and one performs the rite by addressing oneself, one speaks these words from the mind):
"I, bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the summer retreat during the first three months, depending on a certain place and a certain room" (recite this three times).
○ The Method for Receiving the Day [of Retreat] Face-to-Face (After the *an-gu* has been entered,

if there is a matter concerning the Buddha or the Saṃgha, or an invitation from a donor, one’s parents, or others, such that one cannot return on the same day, or must return after two days up to seven days, one should speak thus to a single *bhikṣu*):

"Venerable Sirs, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], having received the seven-day leave, shall go outside the boundary for a certain matter, returning to this very place to observe the rains retreat.
I inform the Venerable Sirs so that they may know. (Recite three times. One should not depart for the sake of food, drink, or clothing.
If it is known that the aforementioned matter will not be concluded within seven days, one should request from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for ten days, half a month, or one month, and then depart.)
The Method for the *Pravāraṇā* (Invitation to Point Out Faults) Among the Assembly of Monks:

(Whenever one has committed an offense, one should first perform confession and only then proceed with the *pravāraṇā*. If there are at least five bhikṣus residing at the monastery, one person should be appointed to receive the *pravāraṇā*.
The others should bare their right shoulders, remove their shoes, kneel with one knee on the ground, join their palms, and address the person receiving the *pravāraṇā*, speaking as follows).
"Venerable Sirs, the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā* today. I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If there is any offense seen, heard, or suspected, may the Venerable Elders, out of compassion, speak to me. If I see an offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
(Recite this three times. If one should speak incorrectly or forget, the person receiving the *pravāraṇā* should grant it one by one.)
○ The Method of *Pravāraṇā* (Invitation to Confession) Before One’s Counterpart (*Pratyekapratimukha-pravāraṇā-dharma*).

(If there are not five bhikṣus residing at the monastery, and one is appointed to receive the *pravāraṇā*, then four bhikṣus shall perform the *pratyekapratimukha-pravāraṇā*. Facing one another, they shall speak as follows.)
"Venerable sirs, please attend to me with one mind. Today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times.

If there are three or two persons, follow this same method, changing only the number of persons addressed. If one has committed an offense and does not confess it, one should not claim to be pure according to the Dharma.)
○ The Method for Mindful Invitation (Pravāraṇā) by Silent Intention (If there is only one person remaining at the residence, one should speak these words while maintaining mental attention):
"Today the Saṃgha performs the invitation ceremony; I, bhikṣu [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times.)

○ The Method for Receiving the Three Robes (The Buddha said: "The three robes should be formally received and maintained. If one possesses robes but does not formally receive them, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense. If ten days pass, one commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, which is difficult to repent for. If there is doubt, one should relinquish them and receive them again. If the color of the robe is red, green, or blue..."
White, black, or those dyed with superior colors do not constitute a valid acceptance; if one obtains a robe of a color that is in accordance with the Dharma, it should be accepted.

○ The Method for Accepting the Antara-vāsaka (The Antara-vāsaka is here translated as "lower garment"). One should maintain dignified deportment and, facing a bhikṣu, or one's upādhyāya or ācārya, speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this five-piece lower robe (antarvāsa), consisting of one long and one short patchwork section, for wearing.
(Recite this three times. If it is from one's upādhyāya, one should address him as 'upādhyāya'; if it is from one's ācārya, one should address him as 'ācārya'.")"
The Method for Receiving the *Uttarāsaṅga* Robe (*Uttarāsaṅga*.
This is translated as "upper garment"; it should be spoken thus):
"Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe. (Twice)
The long is one [unit] and the short is [one unit]. One holds the *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (three recitations).
○ The Ritual for Receiving the *Saṃghāṭī* (the *saṃghāṭī* is translated here as "repeated-layered robe"; it should be spoken thus).

Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am receiving this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips, [number] spans in length and [number] spans in width, as a robe of cut-and-sewn patches. (Recite three times.)
○ The Method for Relinquishing Robes (If there is doubt, one should relinquish them and then receive them again according to the previous method of reception. One should speak as follows):
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe is among my three robes. Previously..."
Having received and maintained [the robe], I now relinquish it (recite this once; then stop. If one wishes to relinquish the other two robes, follow this precedent).
The Method for Receiving the *Nisīdana* (Sitting Mat):
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am receiving this *nisīdana* as my auxiliary garment for the body."
(Recite three times. This is for the purpose of sitting and reclining, not for performing prostrations.
The Method for Receiving a Bowl:
"Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall receive this pātra bowl, which is of the proper measure, for the sake of long-term use."
(Recite three times).
○ The Method for Pure Giving (There are two kinds of pure giving: first, true pure giving; second, successive pure giving).
○ The Ritual for the True Purification of Gifts (This refers to truly relinquishing [the robe] to another; if one wishes to wear it, one must ask that person before wearing it. One should say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], possess this extra robe which has not yet been purified. Now, for the sake of purification—"

Therefore, I relinquish this to the Virtuous One for the sake of true purification (one recitation; the character "cháng" is in the departing tone, pronounced *zhì liàng* [qie-yun], with the sound *zhàng*; it means much, remainder, or surplus).

○ The Method for Successive Pure Gifts (Śuddhaka-dāna) Once a bhikṣu has received the full precepts, all his robes—both new and old—with the exception of the three *kaṣāyas*, must be designated as "pure gifts" (*śuddhaka*) before a trustworthy friend, a fellow bhikṣu who consents, or his two teachers (*upādhyāya* and *ācārya*), acting as the pure donors (*dānapati*).

Taking the robe before one such bhikṣu, he shall recite the name of that pure donor and perform the formal declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-vyākaraṇa*). If he fails to do so and ten days pass, he commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), which requires confession before the Saṃgha. Furthermore, regarding any robes subsequently obtained—even if the cloth is only one foot four inches long and seven inches wide—the same procedure applies.
If one is able to construct a seven-strip robe or a partitioned altar, it must immediately be declared as pure (*śuddha*). One should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], possess this extra robe which has not yet been purified. For the sake of purifying it..."

"Give this to a virtuous one (mahānāma) for the sake of mutual purification. [The recipient of the purification should say: "Virtuous one, you have this extra robe-cloth (*atirekacīvara*) which has not yet been purified.
For the sake of purifying it, give it to me; I now accept it. [Having accepted it, he says: "To whom do you give it? [He replies: "I give it to so-and-so. [The recipient of the purification says:
"Virtuous one, you have this extra robe-cloth which has not yet been purified. For the sake of purifying it, you gave it to me; I have already..."
"I accept it. I give it to [Name]. This robe already belongs to [Name]; you shall properly guard, maintain, and wear it for [Name] according to the circumstances.

(Recite this three times. Afterwards, if one hears that the *śuddhika* master has died or has left the monastic order, one should immediately take all the previously held robes and clothing, designate the name of another *śuddhika* master, and again perform the *śuddhika* dedication.
This text is from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. In the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the text for the *śuddhika* dedication says:)
Venerable sir, please bear this in mind: I, the bhikṣu [name], possess this extra robe which has not yet been formally designated.
It is appropriate that it be so designated; I now designate it in the presence of the venerable one, entrusting it to the bhikṣu [name].

"I now accept this" (recite three times; this constitutes the formal distribution and purification. Even if one does not hear of the death of the donor of the purified gift, or even if they reside in a distant land, the purity of the gift is not lost).

○ The Method for Mentally Renouncing Robes (If one goes abroad on account of matters such as the Three Jewels, intending to return to the residence on that very day, yet encounters difficult circumstances or heavy rain such that bridges are cut off, one should mentally renounce the robes.
It is better to sleep without robes than to commit the *duṣkṛta* offense, which is easily confessed. One should form this mental reflection:)

"I, [Name], having previously received and maintained this robe, now relinquish it. (Recite this once. On the following day, returning to the place where the robe is kept, one should take up the robe before a single bhikṣu, receiving it exactly according to the previous method for taking up a robe.
If all three robes have not been taken away, one should say, "My three robes," and so forth.)

○ The Method for Receiving Non-Timely Medicine (The Buddha permitted the consumption of eight kinds of juices as medicinal drinks when there is a cause for illness—namely, the juices of pear, jujube, sugarcane, grape, lotus root, and so forth. These should first be pressed by a pure person, filtered until clear, and then received from the hand of that pure person.
One should address a single bhikṣu as follows):
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], now for the sake of a certain illness, have this non-time [afternoon] beverage.
In order that it may be consumed outside of the proper time, I now receive it from the venerable one. (Recite three times.)

○ The Method for Receiving Seven-Day Medicine (referring to ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar): Having received these once, one may take them with one’s own hand and consume them for seven days. If they are not finished by the eighth day, one must immediately give them to another; one may not consume them oneself. One should say: [as follows].
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now have the cause of a certain illness;
for this seven-day medicine, because I wish to keep it overnight and consume it over seven days, I now receive it from you, Venerable sir. (Recite three times.)

○ The Method for Receiving Medicine for Life (This refers to pills, powders, and all salty or sour substances that are unfit to be used as food. Once received, one may take and consume them until they are exhausted. One should say:)
Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now have a certain illness as a cause.
This [medicine] [Name] is a medicine for life-long use; because I wish to keep it overnight and take it continuously, I now receive it from you, venerable sir. (Recite three times.)
Appendix (Fifteen Dharma Talks from Nanshan, Lingzhi, and Yunqi, intended to remedy contemporary ills and serve as a means for self-examination).
By Vinaya Master Xuan of Nanshan during the Tang Dynasty:
"The reason why sentient beings have long wandered through the ocean of birth and death is truly due to their lack of the vessel and oars of moral precepts."
It is so. If one boards the vessel of precepts and rows with the oars of compassion, yet is unable to cut across the wind and waves to reach the distant shore, such a thing is impossible.
Therefore, although the orthodox teachings are many, the single precept serves as the foundation of practice.

Just as one must pass through a door to exit, how could one do so without relying on these precepts? Thus, when first giving rise to the aspiration for the Way, one must first recognize this gateway. Regarding...
Regarding the mental states and the manner in which one contemplates and cultivates these practices, the treatise states: "Now, for one who receives the precepts, compassion is the primary duty.

Within the three thousandfold world system—encompassing ten billion suns and moons, extending upward to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception and downward to the Avīci Hell—one must give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all living beings and refrain from killing them, whether for the duration of one's entire life or until the attainment of Buddhahood. Long...

Its temporal categories are universal, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm. This single thought of goodness fills the void of space; its virtue is immeasurable, known only by the Buddha to its ultimate limit.
As it is with non-killing, so it is with all other karmic actions.
Master Yuanzhao of Lingzhi Monastery in Hangzhou, Song Dynasty, whose courtesy name was Zhanran, initially took the Vinaya as his primary field of study.
He held that these precepts were personally instituted by the Buddha himself, descending from Mañjuśrī onwards.
Not even a single word was permitted to be added; when Upāli compiled the collection, he did not dare to expand it by a single character.

Throughout the human and celestial realms, across the ten directions and the triple world within the ocean of lands, the infinite assembly of sages is unified under this same discipline—this may truly be called "strict.

It is like the worldly rites, music, and military expeditions, which must necessarily proceed from the Son of Heaven; the dukes, marquises, ministers, and great officers are not permitted to usurp such authority. Yet, as for the Great Dharma...
Regarding the transmission to the East, it was only the Vinaya that remained unclear; scholars therein had lost their way.

During the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, the Great Vinaya Master Daoxuan of Chengzhao on Mount Zhongnan composed the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the *Jiemoshu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā), and the *Shichao* (Essentials of Monastic Affairs), thereby propagating the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. It has been transmitted [to this day].

More than four hundred years had passed, and nearly sixty schools had produced commentaries on the meaning [of the Vinaya]. Among them, the Vinaya Master Yunkan of Dazhaokong Temple composed the *Huizheng ji* (Record of Rectifying the Teachings), which alone was exhaustive in its reasoning.
Finally, the Vinaya Master Yuanzhao of Lingzhi, known as Dazhi, based his work on the Lotus Sūtra’s revelation of the perfect meaning, composing the *Zichi ji* (Record of Supporting and Sustaining).
This master shared the same ultimate goal, though by different paths, as the Master Huizhen; he further elucidated and promoted [the tradition].
The original intent of Nanshan [Daoxuan] harmonized with the Buddha’s regulations; from this point on, the *Huizheng* and *Zizhi* commentaries further divided the school according to the Vinaya.
It is like splitting a golden staff: the substance of the gold is not lost. How could the unconditioned (*avijñapti*) precept-substance (*śīla-skandha*) possibly be divided? (From the *Xinian lu*).

Thus, the Dharmaguptaka school relies entirely upon the power of Jingkong and Nanshan to propagate it, a tradition that remains uninterrupted to this day. Yet, contemporary students take "mouth-cultivation Chan" to be the means for transcending birth and death; they thus deceive themselves and fall, unlike the ancients.

The teachings of the Dharma have not been transmitted [in this manner]. Formerly, Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an edict stating that monks who had not completed five summer retreats must all study the Vinaya. This emperor’s intention perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind; were it not for a *punar-āgata* bodhisattva coming to assist the orthodox teaching, how could such a thing have been achieved?
(This refers to the Jingkong Monastery in Xiangyang, Yongzhou, where the Vinaya Master Fachong resided.)
Master Yunqi’s *Three Essays from the Bamboo Window*, Part One:
Leaving Home. A former sage once said:
"Leaving home is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish."

Generally, generals establish order through martial prowess, while ministers promote the Great Peace through the arts of literature. The great affairs of the world all issue from the hands of these generals and ministers;
yet, you claim that leaving the household life is not within their capability. If this were so, would leaving the household life then be a trivial matter?
Now, one merely shaves one's hair and dyes one's robes and calls it "leaving the household. Alas! This is nothing more than walking out through two large gates.
This is a home. It is not the home of the burning house of the triple world. Only after leaving the home of the triple world can one be called a Great Man (*mahāsattva*).
Yet that is still not enough. One must leave the triple world together with all sentient beings within it;
only then can one be called a Great Man. As an ancient master sang: "O most excellent son, leaving home is good. The two words 'leaving home' are known to all people."
Few indeed. Those who are the sons of the Most Victorious One are Great Beings (mahāpuruṣa). Great Beings are not easily found;
what wonder, then, that those who even know the two characters for "leaving home" are so few?

When two people first leave the household life, although their aspirations may differ in magnitude, there is none who does not possess a segment of sincere goodness. After a long time, however, they become defiled by the causes and conditions of fame and profit;
consequently, they proceed to construct palatial residences, adorn their clothing, acquire fields and houses, and gather a following of disciples.

They accumulate vast quantities of gold and silk, diligently creating worldly attachments; they are no different from the laity. The Sūtras state that when a single person leaves the home life, Pāpīyas (Māra) is struck with fear.
If things are as they are now, Pāpīyas may well pour wine and offer congratulations! Those who leave the home life with a sincere heart must quickly fix their gaze and see through this clearly.
I have seen ascetic monks practicing austerities in deep mountains who, upon leaving the mountains for the first time, were [beset] by dozens...

If even those men and women with a single grain of faith spend their entire lives buried in worldly affairs by merely taking refuge and making offerings, what need is there to speak of those who are greater?
The ancients said that one must once again leave the home of afflictions and sever the net of worldly toil;

this is "leaving home" after having already left home. It is easy to leave the home one was born into, but difficult to leave the home one has entered as a householder. Because of this, I am filled with anxiety day and night.
Startled.

Regarding the fourfold discernment of those who have left the home life (*pravrajita*), there are those who have left the home life while remaining as householders; those who have left the home life while acting as householders; those who remain as householders while being householders; and those who have left the home life... [text fragment].

One who has left home while remaining within the household—possessing parents, wife, and children, yet whose mind is ever fixed on the Way and untainted by worldly dust—is one who is both at home and has left home.

One who dwells in a monastery, free from the burdens of parents, wife, and children, yet busies himself with fame and profit no differently than a layman—is one who has left home while remaining at home. Such a person dwells among the laity...
Those who abandon [the world] yet remain bound for their entire lives, without a single thought of liberation, are those who dwell at home among householders.
Those who reside in monasteries and exert themselves with diligence for their entire lives, without a single thought of retreat or indolence, are those who have left the home-life among renunciants.
Thus, the four-line verse on "leaving the body and mind behind" by the ancients carries this very meaning. Nevertheless, among those who have left the home-life, there are those of superior capacity.
Let it be as it may. Between being a renunciant and being a householder, it is better to be a householder.
Why? Because to lose one's human form beneath the *kāṣāya* is to fall from the lowest to the lowest.

Regarding the benefits of renunciation, the ancient masters have said: "The most excellent son is one who renounces the world; it is good to leave the household life. There is a common worldly saying:

"If one son renounces the world, the nine generations of his clan will be reborn in heaven. While these all praise renunciation, they do not explicitly clarify the reasons why renunciation constitutes such a benefit.
How could it be said that without plowing or weaving, there is the benefit of natural provision for food and clothing?
How could it be said that without purchasing a house or renting a room, there is the benefit of natural security in one's dwelling?

How could it be said that because kings and ministers protect the Dharma and faithful donors offer respect, one is not conscripted by the government above nor disturbed by the common people below, and thus there is [the benefit of...]?
Yet, what benefit is there in leisure and pleasure? An ancient verse says: "A single grain of rice from a donor is as vast as Mount Sumeru;
if one does not realize the Way for oneself, one shall return wearing fur and bearing horns. It further says:
"In days to come, when the Old Man Yama settles your account for the price of your meals, see how you will respond. This, then, is why leaving the household life is a great matter of concern.
If even those who are subdued [by such a person] are benefited, how much more so those who are truly helped? What is called the benefit of leaving the household life is this:

by destroying afflictions (*kleśa*), severing ignorance (*avidyā*), attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and emerging from the suffering of birth and death, one becomes the most supreme among gods and humans, and one's parents and kinsmen receive its grace.
Otherwise, even if one were as wealthy as a thousand storehouses or as noble as a master...
What benefit is there in these seven emperors? I am truly filled with great sorrow and fear, and thus I inform my fellow practitioners of this together.
It is difficult to renounce the world and bring the mind to rest.

Human nature is such that when cold, one thinks of clothing; when hungry, one thinks of food; in one's dwelling, one thinks of comfort; in one's utensils, one thinks of sufficiency; having a son, one thinks of his marriage;

having a daughter, one thinks of her betrothal; in studying, one thinks of obtaining rank and emolument; in managing a household, one thinks of becoming wealthy and prosperous. At all times, one cannot set these matters aside.
It is for the sake of being free from these burdens that one resolutely leaves the household life; yet, even then, one still does not forget them in various ways.

[The interlocutor] asks: "If this is so, then what is the value of leaving the household life? The Buddha said: "One constantly rubs one's own head to signify the abandonment of finery and ornamentation.
But it is not merely the abandonment of finery; one constantly rubs one's own head, saying: 'I am a monk. Having suddenly cast aside all worldly conditions, one focuses the single mind on the Way."

Outside of monastic affairs, those who study the Confucian tradition take the Six Classics, the Analects, the Mencius, and other such texts as their standard. They prohibit the study of Laozi, Zhuangzi, and even Buddhist scriptures;
that they specialize in their respective fields and find this orthodox principle unremarkable is not to be wondered at. As for being a monk...

It is likewise so. They do not read Buddhist scriptures, but instead read Confucian texts. While reading Confucian texts is not yet considered improper, they go on to read the works of Zhuangzi and Laozi.
Those who are somewhat intelligent further provide commentaries upon them, and subsequently study poetry as well.
To study literature, to study calligraphy, and to study formal correspondence—all such pursuits are signs of the decline of the Dharma, and they cannot be turned back.
The people of this world value cleverness, boast of their extensive learning, and compete for rhetorical elegance; yet these things are not to be relied upon, for they are subject to failure.
There are those who have mastered the hundred schools of thought and whose writings cover the entire age, yet in their next life they may not recognize a single character. This is the extreme case.
Take for example the Elder Chun, who was renowned for his literary talent; yet with a single misstep, he suddenly became demented, a state far worse than even awaiting a future life.
Furthermore, were he to be reborn as a different species—what is called "thinking only of water and grass, knowing nothing else"—wherein would his former reliance be found?
Only the true wisdom of Prajñā, stored within the field of the eight consciousnesses, remains steadfast through all time, unshaken by any fall.

It is not destroyed. Even if one wanders upon the path of delusion, a single touch brings them back to awakening. That people in the secular world do not understand this meaning is not at all surprising;
it is rather lamentable that those who have left the household life take this fundamental matter and set it high on a shelf, while exhausting their efforts in external studies.
How truly remarkable!
Among the various secular affairs of the Sangha,
there were also those who served as geomancers, diviners, physiognomists, and physicians.
Those who act as physicians for gynecology, those who act as masters of talismans, water, incense burners, and alchemy—how extreme is the corruption of the Final Dharma!
Some say that when the Great Master Baizhang ordered the Dhyāna Master Sima to select a site suitable for establishing a monastic center for five hundred monks, he found Mount Wei.
This was a matter of geomancy; subsequently, [Baizhang] ordered him to select [a site] at Wei.
The Master of the Mountain obtained Chan Master Dayou; this was a matter of discerning the family’s destiny. How so? Alas!
This was a great karmic opportunity for the ancient sages to transmit the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, something that cannot be fathomed by worldly people.
As for Baizhang and Sima, what kind of character did they possess? Can the practitioners of divination today use them as mere excuses?
Miscellaneous Arts of the Sangha (2). Some say:
"Miscellaneous arts are certainly not the business of the Sangha; however, since medicine serves to preserve life, it should perhaps be considered unobstructed. I say:
if miscellaneous arts distract the mind, they should be abandoned in all cases. But if one’s intention is to provide relief and succor, then they are but one among the ten thousand practices.
If the technique is not refined, then even though one claims to "preserve life," it will instead result in "injuring life," which is utterly unacceptable.
Recently, there have been monks who practice moxibustion; their method involves making medicinal cakes and placing moxa cones upon them to be ignited, claiming it cures all ailments.
It is unknown from what book this originated or by whom it was transmitted. Indeed, [this involves] cutting into the flesh...
To examine the site and enter the interior by following the channels is the standard method for applying moxibustion with mugwort.
To apply moxibustion through a layer of cake is something that causes pain but lacks efficacy; yet masters practice it, and disciples follow suit, unaware that their craft is profound and weighty.

The difficulty of digesting offerings made out of faith was lamented by Deng Huoqu himself, who said: "Those who act as monks attend only to their own affairs, yet they bring hardship upon the donors of the ten directions;
truly, these offerings are difficult to digest. How true these words are! For a monk concerns himself with his own birth and death, just as a scholar-official concerns himself with his own.
This refers to one's official rank or degree. For the sake of such a rank, one exhausts the resources of one's neighbors and relatives to provide whatever is required;
once the name is achieved, it is sufficient to repay them. If the name is not achieved, the debt incurred is great.
Not understanding this principle, yet only begrudging that offerings from the faithful are not extensive—is this not a grave error?
Regarding the Yunqi Monastic Code on Unreasonable Solicitation for Alms: One who solicits alms unreasonably shall be expelled from the monastery. A monk said: "This does not merit such a prohibition;
to prohibit it would deprive sentient beings of their field of merit. [The Master replied: "Though the individual soliciting unreasonably may personally bear the fault, sentient beings..."
One gains the benefit of overcoming stinginess and relinquishing wealth. Yet, worldly monastics falsely take the name of the Buddha to pursue their livelihood;
when has the Buddha ever issued a prohibition against such people? I replied: "What you say is indeed true, but you know only one side of the matter and not the other.
Those who solicit donations through improper means deceive themselves regarding cause and effect. When donors perceive this, they consequently lose heart."
Thereafter, they ceased giving altogether; how, then, could they have been able to overcome their stinginess? During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were disciples who returned from traveling afar;
when they passed through various villages, the inhabitants closed their doors upon seeing them. When asked the reason, they said it was because they feared the monks’ soliciting for alms.
They reported this to the Buddha, who then rebuked them in various ways. How can one say that [the laity] do not exercise restraint? Be careful!
At Jingzhai Wenzhen Liji Temple, there were two monks, master and disciple, both of whom were reputed for their prudence and integrity.

Entrusted with the performance of sutra recitations and repentance rites, their patrons increased day by day, whereby they became wealthy. Nevertheless, they remained stingy and did not use their wealth for their own enjoyment, nor did they practice charity. Later, they...
He fell ill. His kinsmen welcomed him back to provide medical treatment, but he passed away shortly thereafter. All the wealth he had accumulated throughout his life was taken over by his relatives.

Ten years later, he appeared in a dream to those close to him and said: "Those for whom the recitation of sutras and repentance rites remains incomplete face extremely urgent examinations in the underworld;
the suffering is beyond description. What is transmitted in the human world—that one can recognize characters and read them back amidst a flash of lightning—is indeed not false. [End of] brush.
This was done to admonish those who respond to conditions.
The *Yankou* (Flaming Mouth) food-offering ritual, wherein the Master of Food Offerings initiated the teaching for Ānanda, is subsumed within the Yoga Tantra class. Yoga flourished greatly in...
The two masters of the Tang dynasty, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra, were able to command spirits and deities and to shift mountains and seas;
their power of majestic spirit was inconceivable. After several generations had passed, no one was able to succeed them, and what remained was only the single dharma of *bali* (food offering).
With hands forming mudrās, mouths reciting mantras, and minds performing visualizations, the three karmas were brought into correspondence.
This refers to yoga; its practice is not an easy matter. At present, even the mudras and mantras may not be perfected, let alone the power of visualization.
Thus, they would be inconsistent with the requirements. If they are inconsistent, not only will one fail to benefit sentient beings, but one may even end up harming oneself.
Yesterday, a monk from outside the monastic community in the mountains was already critically ill. That evening, while we were performing the ritual of offering food (gandha-bali), he said, "Look..."
The patient said, "A ghost seized me and tried to take me out to eat. I refused to go. Suddenly it came again and said, 'Dharma Master, you are not sincere;
we have returned empty-handed. You shall surely be made to pay for this. Thereupon, it grabbed my arm and led me away.
The crowd held poles, hooks, and snares, saying they wished to drag this Dharma Master down to the ground. I was terrified and cried out for help. (1)
At that time, they dispersed. Several days later, the monk died; it was because even before his death, he had already been in the company of the ghosts.
Had he not shouted out then, would the Master on the platform not have been in peril? This is not all. One monk, lacking sincerity, was carried by ghosts to a river to be drowned.
Another monk lost the key to his clothing chest, yet kept the key in mind. When the ghosts saw his food...
Above [the food] were all iron shards, so that he could not eat. Another monk had left his felt robe out to dry and had not yet put it away when it began to rain;
he kept his mind focused on this robe. The ghosts saw that the food atop their bowls had become nothing but animal fur, so they too could not eat.

Each received a manifest retribution. Furthermore, one man entered the underworld and saw several hundred monks in a black room; their bodies were emaciated and their complexions haggard, appearing as if...

Their appearance was one of unbearable grief and suffering. When questioned, they were all *śrāddha* masters (those who perform food-offerings). Truly, it is not an easy matter to perform these food-offerings!
[This concludes] the miscellaneous anecdotes regarding the recitation of scriptures.
General Qi, who had long been a devotee of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, was serving as the governor of Sanjiang in Yue. A deceased soldier appeared to him in a dream, saying:
"Tomorrow I shall send my wife to you to beg that you recite one scroll of the sūtra for her benefit in the afterlife.
The following day, a woman indeed came weeping to seek an audience. When questioned, her words were exactly as they had been in the dream. The General consented; rising at dawn, he recited it.

One night, he dreamed that the spirit-soldier said, "I am grateful for your great kindness, Master; however, I have obtained only half a scroll, as it contains the two characters 'not used' (*fuyō*) interspersed within it.
The Master pondered the reason for this. Then, while an attendant was sending tea and cakes to him, the Master saw her from afar and waved his hand to dismiss her.
Although he did not speak, his heart meant that they were not needed. The next morning, he closed his room and recited the sutra. That night, the spirit-soldier appeared again in a dream.

Xie said: "I have already attained transcendence and deliverance. This I heard personally from the monk Donglin of Sanjiang, who was sincere, possessed of spiritual practice, and one who did not speak falsely.
Alas! Should not monks who recite the sutras be cautious?"
Daoji criticized those who followed the teachings of Śākyamuni, saying: "The various palaces, observatories, Daoist academies, and shrines to the gods are all our dwellings.
Why is it that so many monks reside within them, while we followers of the Dao rarely see anyone living in Buddhist temples? Indeed, those who take refuge in the Buddha should reside in monasteries."
"Those who take refuge in the Way reside in palaces, pavilions, monasteries, and temples; now the monks dwell here.

Are they taking refuge in the Three Clarities, the various Celestial Honored Ones, the various Perfected Beings, or the spirits? Or do they intend to seize our property? These words were indeed reasonable.
I had no reply. After a moment, he said slowly, "Taoguang, you are from Gulingyin. Why would a follower of the Way reside there?
I replied, "This is where those practicing the Complete Perfection (Quanzhen) while remaining laypeople reside. Those who wear crowns and hairpins do not dwell there;
moreover, a single tonsured monk presides over it. His words were reasonable, and I again had no reply. Alas! Among those who are monks today, some reside...

One may reside in a monastic community, dwell in seclusion at an araṇya, take up residence in a cave as one's chamber, or build a thatched hut beneath a tree—what is there that would not be acceptable?
Yet why must one necessarily attach oneself to those in clerical robes to serve as the host of a dwelling?

At present, the monasteries in various regions each have their own records of the precepts (*śīla-piṭaka*), yet they do not recount the origins of how the precepts were obtained or the essential points regarding observance and violation.

They merely record the names of the three masters and seven witnesses, as well as those who received the precepts on the same altar and at the same time, along with the administrative head (*karmadāna*).
The titles of the Vice Abbot, the Guest Prefect, the Treasurer, and so forth, have no bearing on the matter at hand.
If you wish to record them, you should record the five patriarchs of the Abbot, as well as his year of birth, his *kalpa* (years since ordination), and his place of birth.

I received the full precepts from Master Shanshan.
In the various Vinaya texts, there is no mention of a *śrāmaṇera-ācārya* for shaving the hair; originally, the act of shaving was performed by someone sent by the *upādhyāya*.
In recent times, those ignorant of the legal codes have further erroneously added the office of a *śīla-parīkṣaka-ācārya*, citing [unfounded] invitations.
The Ācārya. The *zhìtán* (坛) Ācārya refers to the original *shěnjiè* (审戒) instructor, who is identical to the *jiàoshòu* (教授) instructor.

First, outside the maṇḍala, they complete the interrogation regarding various impediments (*āvaraṇa*). Next, they are led into the interior of the maṇḍala. After the *Karmavācanā* master has interrogated them before the assembly, he then performs the four *karmas* to confer the precepts.
The *zhìtán* [Ācārya] refers to the person receiving the precepts who has first arrived and is not yet familiar with the ritual protocols.

Fearing that one might hastily lose proper decorum when presiding over the altar, the ritual procedures were thus established. There is no position for an *ācārya* (Sanskrit: *ācārya*; Chinese: "model teacher" or "preceptor") in these rites.
Even among the seven witnesses at the altar, there is no such rank as a teacher; they are simply referred to as the "seven-witness *saṃgha*.
How much more so for those who are not? The Buddha stated: "To call someone an *upādhyāya* who is not an *upādhyāya*, or to call someone an *ācārya* [who is not an *ācārya*]..."
To address someone as "Ācārya" when they are not, or to address them by both titles [when they do not qualify for either], constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).

(Those who act as disciples must preserve this record so that future generations may know their teacher’s year of birth and seniority in the precepts. If there are no followers, it may then be burned.)
